4.1 - Prototype Inheritance: Prototype inheritance is the mechanism by which objects in JavaScript inherit properties and methods from other objects. Every JavaScript object has an internal link to another object called its prototype, accessible as __proto__. When you access a property on an object and JavaScript cannot find it directly on that object, it walks up the prototype chain automatically until it either finds the property or reaches null at the top of the chain. This prototype lookup is invisible to you but happens on every single property access.

Think of prototype inheritance as a delegation chain, not a copy. If object A has object B as its prototype, and you look for a method on A that does not exist there, JavaScript automatically delegates the lookup to B. This chain continues all the way up to Object.prototype which is the root. The key insight is that objects do not copy properties from their prototype. They delegate lookups to it at runtime. This delegation model is what makes prototype inheritance both powerful and memory-efficient. All instances share one copy of inherited methods rather than each having their own copy.

When you use the class syntax in modern JavaScript it is still prototype-based inheritance under the hood. The class keyword is purely syntactic sugar. When you write class Dog extends Animal, JavaScript sets up the prototype chain so that Dog.prototype has Animal.prototype as its prototype. The instanceof operator also relies on this chain to check if an object was derived from a particular constructor function. Understanding the prototype chain helps you debug unexpected behavior when properties seem to appear from nowhere or when you accidentally shadow a prototype method.
2.2 - WebSocket Handshake: A WebSocket connection begins with something called the handshake, and it starts as a regular HTTP request. The browser sends a GET request to the server but includes a special header: Upgrade: websocket. It also includes a Sec-WebSocket-Key header which is a randomly generated base64-encoded value. The browser is essentially asking the server to upgrade this HTTP connection to a persistent WebSocket connection. This is why WebSocket URLs start with ws:// or wss:// but the initial handshake itself travels over HTTP.

When the server receives the upgrade request it responds with HTTP 101 Switching Protocols. It takes the client's Sec-WebSocket-Key, concatenates a fixed GUID string to it, hashes the result with SHA-1, and base64 encodes it. This becomes the Sec-WebSocket-Accept response header. The client verifies this value to confirm it is talking to a genuine WebSocket server and not a misconfigured proxy. Once the 101 response is received, the HTTP connection is upgraded and both sides can now send frames in either direction at any time without the request-response overhead of HTTP.

After the WebSocket handshake completes, the connection becomes a full-duplex channel. Unlike HTTP where the client must always initiate a request, with WebSocket the server can push data to the client at any time. Data is sent in frames rather than complete HTTP messages, which makes it much more efficient for real-time applications like chat, live dashboards, or collaborative editing. The connection stays open until either side explicitly closes it with a close frame, or the network drops.
5.1 - V8 Engine and Hidden Classes: V8, the JavaScript engine inside Node.js and Chrome, uses hidden classes to optimize property access on objects. When you create an object and add properties to it, V8 creates an internal hidden class that describes the shape of that object. Hidden classes are similar to structs in C. Every time you add a new property to an object V8 creates a new hidden class and transitions the object to it. This is how V8 avoids the overhead of a hash table lookup on every property access and can instead use fast fixed-offset memory access.

The critical thing to understand about V8 hidden classes is that two objects that look identical to you can end up with completely different hidden classes if you add properties in a different order. If you create object A and add x then y, and create object B and add y then x, V8 sees them as different shapes and cannot optimize them the same way. This also means dynamically adding properties after object construction, especially in conditionals or loops, causes hidden class transitions that hurt performance significantly in hot code paths.

To write V8-friendly code, always initialize all object properties in the constructor in the same order every time. Never add new properties to an object after construction if you can avoid it. Avoid delete operator on properties as it forces V8 to switch to a slower dictionary mode. Prefer setting a property to null instead of deleting it. When you follow these patterns V8 can share hidden classes across all instances of the same constructor, leading to significant speedups through inline caching and JIT compilation.
3.2 - Memoization and Computed State: Memoization is an optimization technique where you cache the result of an expensive computation and return the cached result when the same inputs occur again instead of recomputing. In React, useMemo lets you memoize the result of a computation and only recompute it when its dependencies change. This is particularly valuable for computed state that derives from props or other state values and would otherwise be recalculated on every render even when the inputs have not changed.

useMemo and useCallback are both memoization hooks but they serve different purposes. useMemo memoizes a computed value while useCallback memoizes a function reference. You need useCallback when you pass callbacks to child components that are themselves wrapped in React.memo, because without memoizing the callback the child still re-renders since it receives a new function reference on every parent render. The combination of React.memo on the child component and useCallback on the parent's callback prop is the complete pattern for preventing unnecessary child renders.

Memoization helps computed state because it prevents redundant work during renders. If you have a filtered and sorted list derived from a large array of items, and the filter or sort criteria have not changed, there is no reason to redo that work. Without useMemo the filter and sort run on every render even when unrelated state updates trigger a re-render. With useMemo the computation is skipped entirely if the dependencies have not changed. The main pitfall is over-memoizing: adding useMemo everywhere without profiling first adds overhead from the dependency comparison that can actually be slower than just recomputing.
6.1 - The Event Loop and Microtasks: JavaScript runs on a single thread, so it can only do one thing at a time. The event loop is the mechanism that lets it stay responsive despite that. There is a call stack where function calls are pushed and popped, and a task queue (the macrotask queue) where callbacks from things like setTimeout, I/O, and DOM events wait. The event loop has one simple rule: when the call stack is empty, take the next task from the queue and run it to completion. 'Run to completion' is key — a task is never interrupted halfway, which is why long synchronous work freezes the page.

Promises do not use the macrotask queue. They use a separate, higher-priority microtask queue. After every single task finishes and before the event loop picks up the next macrotask, it completely drains the microtask queue. This is why a resolved Promise's .then callback always runs before a setTimeout(fn, 0) scheduled at the same time — microtasks jump the line. The practical consequence: if you schedule microtasks that themselves schedule more microtasks, you can starve the macrotask queue and block rendering. await is just syntax over .then, so the code after an await also runs as a microtask.
3.1 - Long-Polling vs WebSockets: Before WebSockets, the common trick for real-time updates was long-polling. The client sends an HTTP request and the server deliberately holds it open instead of responding immediately. When data becomes available, the server responds, and the client instantly sends another request to wait again. It simulates a push, but every message still pays the full cost of an HTTP request and response — new headers, sometimes a new TCP connection — and there is always a gap between responses where the client is reconnecting.

A WebSocket replaces all of that with a single long-lived, full-duplex TCP connection. After the initial HTTP Upgrade handshake, both sides can send frames at any time with only a few bytes of framing overhead — no repeated headers, no reconnect gap. This makes WebSockets dramatically more efficient for high-frequency, bidirectional traffic like chat, live cursors, or trading data. Long-polling still has its place: it is simpler, works through old proxies, and is fine for low-frequency updates where a dedicated connection per client would be wasteful.
4.1 - React.memo and useCallback: By default a React component re-renders whenever its parent re-renders, even if its props did not change. React.memo wraps a component and skips the re-render when its props are shallowly equal to the previous render. The catch is shallow equality: primitives compare by value, but objects, arrays, and functions compare by reference. If a parent creates a new function or object literal on every render and passes it as a prop, React.memo sees a brand-new reference each time and re-renders anyway, defeating the optimization.

useCallback and useMemo exist to keep references stable across renders. useCallback returns the same function instance as long as its dependency array does not change, and useMemo does the same for a computed value. Wrapping a callback in useCallback before passing it to a React.memo child means the child actually sees a stable prop and can skip re-rendering. The rule of thumb: memoizing is only worth it when the child is expensive to render or the reference is consumed by a memoized child — wrapping everything adds overhead and dependency bugs for no benefit.
